name: r2-all-2
statement: The base's accuracy at a sampling setting is not set by the per-token surprise of its text against any optimum: accuracy rises linearly with surprise and has no peak. A progress step holds its probability in one sequence and beats a restatement, whose mass is split over many paraphrases, and a restatement already in context weakens the next copy instead of reinforcing it, so there is no boredom trap; high surprise explores alternatives instead of drifting, so there is no confusion trap. Loops come from the sampler's tail, not from low surprise: rare tail tokens knock the base off its progress line into a stock reasoning block that it then re-enters. The opening cue moves the base into a higher-entropy exploratory mode, which is why the cue loops more than the plain prompt at T 0.6 (more tail mass to fall into), why it is worth more at T 1.0 (exploration pays when surprise is high), and why any mode-sharpening truncation (top-p < 1, min-p) helps the cued base but costs the plain base at T 1.0.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base, plain and cued, and Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math, on MATH-500 and the 328 at cap 16,384, sampling with temperature 0.6-1.5 and top-p, min-p or similar truncation, grader v3. Covers cap hits, loops, unextractable answers and the cue-by-sampler interaction. RL is inside the law: it shares the base's tail-driven loop mechanism and responds to truncation the same way, and its temperature flatness reflects tail mass and surprise moving together, not immunity. It does not cover weight edits.

explains.how: At T 0.6 with top-p 0.95 the cued base's exploratory mode still places mass on tail tokens, and the low temperature keeps it from exploring its way back out once a tail token has pushed it into a stock block, so long answers run to the cap.
The +24 from removing top-p at T 0.6 is not tail recovery: the difference is inside its own interval [-0.7, 10.3], and the 98 cap hits show the untruncated tail still feeding loops at the same rate.

At T 1.0 surprise is high and accuracy follows it up linearly; the cue's exploratory mode turns that surprise into new progress steps, and the remaining 27 cap hits are tail excursions that truncation would remove.
The plain base at T 0.6 has half the cued base's cap hits because its lower-entropy mode puts less mass in the tail, the factor that actually starts loops.

At T 1.0 the cue's higher-entropy mode turns extra surprise into exploration while the plain base's low-entropy mode cannot use it; at T 0.6 there is little surprise to exploit, so the cue gains only 3-10 points.

explains.quote: Plain base: T 1.0 - T 0.6 = -28.0, -29.6, -27.2, 0.0 by quartile
explains.how: The plain base's loss at higher T is a tail effect, not drift: its low-entropy mode samples junk tail tokens at T 1.0 on short problems, while on the longest problems the gain in surprise pays off in exploration and offsets that loss exactly.
On the 328 the same split holds: the cued exploratory mode gains from added surprise (119 to 164) and the plain low-entropy mode loses to tail tokens (107 to 76).
Harder problems keep the base longer, so it meets more tail tokens; raising T lets the exploratory mode climb back out of stock blocks, halving the cap hits.

explains.quote: the base's loops have periods of hundreds of characters
explains.how: The loops are whole stock reasoning blocks the base is knocked into by a tail token, not a copy-by-copy build-up of the last sentence; their length is set by the stock block, not by reinforcement.

The base's own prefix was written by its exploratory sampler and already contains tail-token deflections; RL's prefix has none, so the continuation finishes from RL's prefix and not from its own, with the number of copies in context playing no part.

explains.quote: cuts limit loops 59 -> 53, T 1 cuts to 24
explains.how: In an unrelated model the loop count depends on the specific sampler setting, not on one surprise value, as a sampler-specific tail law predicts.

conflicts.how: At T 1.0 the cued base still has non-loop cap hits on RL-only problems; the theory calls these long tail-token excursions without independent evidence that the tail started them.
If accuracy rises linearly with surprise, RL should gain from T 0.6 to T 1.0; the theory has to argue that RL's tail cost and surprise gain cancel exactly.

conflicts.quote: Rule-A loops: 0 of 500 in either cell
conflicts.how: With zero loops at T 1.0 the tail law has no loops left to remove, yet the theory still credits truncation with a gain there.

rival: Accuracy has a single optimum in per-token surprise: low surprise traps the base in self-reinforcing restatement loops and high surprise makes it drift, and the cue lowers the base's entropy, so mode-sharpening truncation at T 1.0 pushes the cued base back toward loops while rescuing the plain base from drift. Separation: under the rival, top-p 0.95 at T 1.0 adds about 18 cap hits to the cued base, costs it about 12 points and raises the plain base by about 38; under this theory top-p 0.95 at T 1.0 removes tail-started cap hits from the cued base (fewer than 27), raises it above 410, and costs the plain base points below 224. The sign of the truncation effect on each prompt separates the two.

predictions.experiment: Base + opening cue, MATH-500 n=500, T 1.0 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: cap hits
predictions.refuted_by: 33 or more cap hits (truncating the tail at T 1.0 brings loops back)

predictions.experiment: Same run (base + cue, MATH-500, T 1.0 / top-p 0.95): right
Plain base (no cue), MATH-500 n=500, T 1.0 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: right (plain T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 is 224)
predictions.refuted_by: 240 or more right (truncation rescues the plain base)

predictions.experiment: Base + opening cue, the 328 harder problems, T 1.0 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: cap hits (top-p 1.0 gives 77)
Plain base (no cue), MATH-500 n=500, T 0.8 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, one sample, grader v3: right (T 0.6 gives 305-319, T 1.0 gives 224)
predictions.refuted_by: 290 or more right (a peak between T 0.6 and T 1.0)

predictions.experiment: Teacher-forced under the base: mean per-token surprise (negative log-probability at T 1) of the cued base's 500 MATH-500 answers at T 1.0, after the cue, divided by that of the plain base's 500 answers at T 1.0 (existing answers)
predictions.refuted_by: ratio 0.9 or less (the cue moves the base to a lower-entropy mode)

imports.finding: Repetition rate depends on the sampling method itself and not on one value of the observed cross-entropy of generated text; quality rises with surprise without a boredom trap at the low end or a confusion trap at the high end.
imports.how: Explains the cue-by-temperature interaction the team never explained (cue +38.6 at T 1.0 but small at T 0.6, cued base loops more than plain at T 0.6) as exploration paying off at high surprise, and predicts that top-p 0.95 at T 1.0 helps the cued base and costs the plain base.

imports.finding: Loops arise when a low-probability action knocks a model off its progress path into a cyclic block; the progress action keeps its mass in one sequence, so sharpening favours progress; harder problems loop more only because they run longer and meet more tail tokens; truncating the tail removes loops.
imports.how: Explains why tail truncation removes loops, why the 328 shows more cap hits than MATH-500, and predicts that loops and cap hits fall further at T 1.0 under top-p 0.95 or min-p.

imports.finding: The probability of repeating a sentence falls with the number of copies already in context, rising linearly with nothing; high-probability sentences are the least likely to be repeated.
imports.how: Explains why a run's length to the 16,384 cap is set by the stock block it fell into, and why the base's own prefix finishes less often (23) than RL's (48): deflections in the prefix, not copies, decide it.
